items.title: Camera Upgrades for 3D Printers
items.summary: 3D printing has come a long way over the years, from being a fussy, barely usable mess to essentially being plug-and-play for a large variety of plastics. And the industry tends to cater to makers and hackers as well, with the printers mostly being easily upgradable and even the firmware for them often being open source. [Sam] tested these concepts to the extreme with his Prusa Core One. The printer does have an open-source firmware and will even somewhat automatically accommodate a camera if one is plugged in, but he wanted it to do a few extra things and went through 42 firmware revisions to get it just right . The first upgrade was to the camera hardware. The ESP32-S3-based camera has an autofocus feature, so that was the first thing to build in. From there it needed access to an SD card to support taking timelapse videos of the prints. This was surprisingly complicated and delved into the intricacies of filesystems but eventually this was solved as well. From there, [Sam] tackled issues with digital zoom, exposures randomly changing and washing out the image, and then finally on to making sure the timelapse feature was easy to use and reliable. This is the feature he uses the most on his printers, so he made it auto-start the recording and also made the recording process more robust to power outages. With all of that, [Sam] has an upgraded camera for his Prusa printers that dramatically improves quality and reliability. And the fact that these printers are among those that are more open and easier to work on certainly facilitated that journey. To that end, his own firmware is available on his GitHub page , and if you’re unlucky enough to have a printer which doesn’t abide by the open ethos of other printers, there will always be community solutions to those problems

items.title: Daisy Chaining Stepper Motors
items.summary: Let’s say you want to control a whole bunch of stepper motors. You can use a multi-channel controller board, or whip something up with a microcontroller or two. Or, you could look at [Josh Rogan’s] design for a system of daisy chainable stepper motors that can all be controlled together. The idea is simple enough—give each stepper motor a smart controller that can accept commands and also pass them on to other units in a daisy chain. It’s not unlike the idea behind addressable LED strings, but with stepper motors instead. [Josh] refers to it as the CANBUS Stepper project, and it’s designed for NEMA 17 steppers—putting everything necessary to drive one into a single compact board that sits on the back of the motor itself. It’s built around the ESP32-S3 microcontroller, and the TCM2209 stepper driver chip. It’s intended that one node will be hooked up over USB, Wi-Fi, Serial, or CAN, and the rest of the steppers in the chain get commands passed down from the first node as needed. We’ve seen [Josh]’s work before, too— with his earlier development of USB-PD powered steppers . It’s well worth checking out if you’re into this sort of thing. Video after the break. Marring this memorable occasion is the disconcerting discovery that although the spacecraft is still sending a carrier wave back to Earth via the Deep Space Network (DSN), it’s no longer sending science- and engineering data , with the cause still to be determined. This is reminiscent of the 2023 incident in which Voyager 1 went completely silent aside from the carrier signal, before being coaxed back to life. Following this, a defective flight data system (FDS) RAM chip was remotely diagnosed and bypassed. items.title: First Smartphone? Think Blue
items.summary: High-tech for the 90s. “ IBM Simon Personal Communicator ” by [Bcos47] If you ask most people when the smartphone arrived, they will usually say 2007 with the first iPhone. Others might argue for a BlackBerry or a Nokia Communicator. But the IBM Simon Personal Communicator beats them all. It wasn’t even close. This early smartphone went on sale on August 16, 1994, more than twelve years before the iPhone, and it already had the defining features we now take for granted: a touch screen, applications, electronic mail, and a single device that was both a telephone and a small computer. Simon started as a prototype code-named Sweetspot, at COMDEX two years earlier. It was the brainchild of IBM engineer [Frank Canova]. The prototype could make calls, send faxes, electronic mail, and cellular pages, and it had services such as maps, stocks, and news that would not be ordinary phone apps for years. IBM refined the design as Angler, and the finished product got its final name from BellSouth, which would sell it. Simon was reportedly a nod to Simon Says, because the device was supposed to do what you told it to do. IBM didn’t build the phone, however. That was left to Mitsubishi Electric. Informally, many people called it a “ThinkPhone” in a nod to the famous IBM Think sign that was always somewhere around an IBM mainframe. Inside, Simon was an 8086 computer. It used an NEC V30HL processor running at 16 MHz. It sported a whopping one megabyte of RAM, one megabyte of flash storage, a PCMCIA slot for expansion, and it ran Datalight ROM-DOS under a touch interface called Navigator. No DOS prompt in sight. Surf-Roll is exactly that — it simulates feelings of slippery and sticky by changing how fast a touched surface moves, relative to the one touching it. The basic idea is this: when one drags their fingertip across a surface, there’s an expectation that the surface will slide under their skin at a certain rate. Researchers discovered that if the surface moves faster than expected, it’s perceived as slippery. If it moves slower than expected, it creates a feeling of sticky. Surf-Roll demonstrates this in virtual reality with dabs of virtual “oil” and “honey”, and a small handheld device with a wheel to deliver the sensations. The viewer’s fingertip rests on the surface of the wheel, and the device rotates it at a rate depending on what the user is touching in VR. If the viewer is touching nothing, the wheel does not spin. But when dragging their fingertip across a virtual tabletop and through virtual gobs of honey or oil, it spins the wheel to match the sensations required. It’s an interesting effect, demonstrated with a relatively simple prototype. It’s a kind of physical illusion. Most illusions are visual in nature, but some involve other senses . items.title: Did the user ask for this? Securing AI agents against intent hijacking with Semantic governance policies
items.summary: Semantic governance policies protect AI agents from indirect prompt injection and intent hijacking by validating every proposed tool call against user intent and natural language constraints before execution. Developers can leverage these policies in preview within the Gemini platform via Agent Gateway to secure tool-use workflows.

items.title: Check what your AI agents do before they do it, with Semantic governance policies

items.summary: Agent Anomaly Detection now monitors ADK agents running across AWS, Azure, or on-premises by analyzing their traces and logs in your Google Cloud project. By ingesting OpenTelemetry-formatted data through the Telemetry API, it evaluates full conversations for behavioral drift without needing access to the agent's underlying runtime. This enables security teams to detect risks like rogue behaviors, tool misuse, and resource exhaustion across multi-cloud environments.

items.title: Announcing Long-Context Training on TPUs with MaxText Context Parallelism
items.summary: Google Cloud's MaxText framework now supports long-context training up to 14 million tokens on Cloud TPUs by implementing four context-parallel strategies: All-gather, A2A, P2P, and USP. Powered by the Tokamax Splash Attention kernel, these strategies effectively manage attention compute and memory bottlenecks without materializing full key-value sequences in high-bandwidth memory. Developers can adopt these capabilities in MaxText v0.2.4 to achieve high Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) across large-scale model training workflows.
